questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A map has a scale of 1:25,000. What actual ground distance, in kilometres, does a straight-line distance of 8 cm on the map represent?
options: 2 km
20 km
8 km
questions.explanation: Ground distance = 8 cm x 25,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 m = 2 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A road measuring 6 km on the ground is shown as 12 cm on a map. What is the scale of the map, expressed as a representative fraction?
questions.explanation: 6 km = 600,000 cm. Scale = map distance : ground distance = 12 : 600,000 = 1 : 50,000.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A rectangular plot of farmland measures 4 cm by 3 cm on a map drawn to a scale of 1:20,000. What is the actual area of the plot in square kilometres?
options: 4.8 km squared
0.12 km squared
12 km squared
0.48 km squared
questions.explanation: Ground length = 4 cm x 20,000 = 80,000 cm = 0.8 km; ground width = 3 cm x 20,000 = 60,000 cm = 0.6 km. Area = 0.8 x 0.6 = 0.48 km squared.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The bearing of a village Q from a town P is 128 degrees. What is the bearing of P from Q (the back bearing)?
options: 308 degrees
052 degrees
128 degrees
232 degrees
questions.explanation: Since the given bearing (128 degrees) is less than 180 degrees, add 180: 128 + 180 = 308 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The bearing of a hilltop R from a camp S is 205 degrees. What is the bearing of S from R?
options: 205 degrees
155 degrees
385 degrees
025 degrees
questions.explanation: Since the given bearing (205 degrees) exceeds 180 degrees, subtract 180: 205 - 180 = 25 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A surveyor walks due North for 3 km from point A to point B, then due East for 4 km from B to C. What is the straight-line (direct) distance from A to C?
options: 12 km
7 km
1 km
5 km
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras: AC = square root of (3 squared + 4 squared) = square root of 25 = 5 km, since the North and East legs form a right angle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, two points 3 km apart horizontally have a height difference of 90 m. What is the gradient between them, expressed as a ratio?
questions.explanation: Gradient = height difference / horizontal distance = 90 m / 3,000 m = 1:33.3 (approximately).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Two points on a map are 1,500 m apart. Contours show one point at 250 m and the other at 175 m above sea level. What is the gradient between them?
questions.explanation: Height difference = 250 - 175 = 75 m. Gradient = 75/1,500 = 1/20, or 1:20.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A hill has an average gradient of 1:25 along a slope that rises 60 m in elevation. What is the approximate horizontal distance covered by this slope?
questions.explanation: Gradient 1:25 means for every 1 m of rise, there are 25 m of horizontal distance. Horizontal distance = 60 x 25 = 1,500 m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a map, contour lines that form a set of concentric circles with values increasing inward most likely represent a
options: coastal lagoon
hill or conical elevation
river valley or depression
flat plain
questions.explanation: Concentric contour circles with increasing values toward the centre indicate rising ground, characteristic of a hill or conical summit.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a map, contour lines that form a V-shape pointing towards higher ground (with the point of the V crossing a stream) typically indicate a
options: plateau
hilltop
river valley
escarpment edge only
questions.explanation: Where contours form a V that points upslope (upstream) across a stream line, this indicates a river valley, since rivers erode a channel into the surrounding higher ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A map is described as an 'enlargement' of another map when its scale is
options: converted from a linear scale to a statement scale only
kept exactly the same but redrawn on larger paper
decreased, for example from 1:25,000 to 1:50,000
increased, for example from 1:50,000 to 1:25,000
questions.explanation: Enlarging a map increases its representative fraction (making the second number smaller), so 1:50,000 enlarged becomes a larger-scale map such as 1:25,000.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following statements about a 'small-scale' map is correct?
options: It always has a representative fraction larger than 1:10,000
It covers a large area of the ground with relatively little detail
It cannot be used to show contour lines
It covers a small area of the ground with a great deal of detail
questions.explanation: A small-scale map (e.g., 1:1,000,000) has a small representative fraction and shows a large ground area but with less detail than a large-scale map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In estimating the area of an irregular lake shown on a map using the grid-square method, a surveyor should count
options: only the fully covered squares, ignoring partial squares entirely
the total number of grid lines crossing the lake
all full squares, plus half of the squares that are only partially covered
only the partially covered squares
questions.explanation: The standard grid-square estimation method sums all fully enclosed squares and adds roughly half the count of partially covered squares to approximate the true area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A Global Positioning System (GPS) device determines a user's location primarily by
options: measuring local atmospheric pressure only
detecting variations in the Earth's magnetic field only
calculating distances from signals received from multiple orbiting satellites
counting the number of nearby triangulation stations
questions.explanation: GPS receivers calculate position by measuring the time delay of signals from at least four satellites, using trilateration to pinpoint latitude, longitude, and elevation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In a Geographic Information System (GIS), 'remote sensing' most accurately refers to
options: manually digitising a paper map using a computer mouse
gathering data about the Earth's surface using satellites or aircraft without direct physical contact
conducting a ground survey using a theodolite
interviewing local residents about land use
questions.explanation: Remote sensing collects information about surface features from a distance, typically via satellite or aerial imagery, feeding directly into GIS databases.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, a settlement located where a river's V-shaped valley opens out into a broad, flat floodplain would most likely be sited for
options: defence on an isolated, steep hilltop
isolation from all transport routes
access to flat, fertile, easily farmed land and a reliable water source
avoidance of any water supply
questions.explanation: Floodplain sites are attractive for settlement because they offer flat land for farming and building, fertile alluvial soils, and easy access to water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A statement scale such as 'one centimetre represents one kilometre' corresponds to a representative fraction of
questions.explanation: 1 km = 100,000 cm, so 1 cm representing 1 km gives a representative fraction of 1:100,000.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a linear (graphical) scale bar showing 0 to 5 km divided into 5 equal segments, a distance measured as 3.5 segments corresponds to
options: 5 km
1.5 km
8.5 km
3.5 km
questions.explanation: Since each full segment on the bar represents 1 km, 3.5 segments directly correspond to 3.5 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate practical method for determining the height of a distant, inaccessible hill from a known baseline?
options: Estimating visually from a photograph
Measuring the hill's shadow length only, without any angle measurement
Counting the number of contour lines crossed while walking around its base
Using a theodolite to measure angles of elevation from two known points and applying trigonometry
questions.explanation: Trigonometric levelling, using angle-of-elevation readings from a theodolite at two known points along a measured baseline, is the standard practical method for determining inaccessible heights.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A cross-section (relief profile) drawn between two points on a topographical map is primarily used to
options: show the location of settlements only
determine the area enclosed by contour lines
show the shape of the land surface (relief) along a straight line between the two points
calculate the exact bearing between the two points
questions.explanation: A cross-section transfers the heights indicated by contours along a chosen line onto a graph, visually representing the rise and fall of the land surface between the two points.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A place P is located at longitude 75 degrees East. If it is 12 noon at Greenwich (0 degrees), what is the local time at P?
options: 12 noon
questions.explanation: Time difference = 75/15 = 5 hours ahead, since P is east of Greenwich. 12 noon + 5 hours = 5:00 pm.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A town X is located at longitude 105 degrees West. If it is 12 noon at Greenwich, what is the local time at X?
options: 12 noon
questions.explanation: Time difference = 105/15 = 7 hours behind, since X is west of Greenwich. 12 noon - 7 hours = 5:00 am.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Two towns lie on the same latitude. Town A is at longitude 20 degrees East and Town B is at longitude 50 degrees East. What is the time difference between them, and which is ahead?
options: 2 hours; A is ahead of B
6 hours; B is ahead of A
30 hours; B is ahead of A
2 hours; B is ahead of A
questions.explanation: Difference in longitude = 50 - 20 = 30 degrees; time difference = 30/15 = 2 hours. Since B is further east, B's local time is ahead of A's.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A ship's clock reads 9:00 am when it is 3:00 pm at Greenwich. What is the ship's approximate longitude?
options: 22.5 degrees West
90 degrees West
90 degrees East
45 degrees West
questions.explanation: Time difference = 6 hours behind Greenwich, meaning the ship is west. Longitude = 6 x 15 = 90 degrees West.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: It is 4:00 pm on Monday at a location on longitude 60 degrees East. What is the local time at a location on longitude 45 degrees West on the same day?
options: 11:00 pm the previous day
1:00 am the next day
questions.explanation: Total longitude difference = 60 + 45 = 105 degrees; time difference = 105/15 = 7 hours. Since 45 degrees West is behind 60 degrees East, subtract 7 hours from 4:00 pm to get 9:00 am.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A location lies exactly on the International Date Line. Crossing it from west to east (for example, from Asia towards the Americas) requires a traveller to
options: add a day to the calendar date
subtract a day from the calendar date
make no adjustment at all
add 12 hours only, with no date change
questions.explanation: Travelling eastward across the International Date Line moves a traveller back one calendar day, compensating for the cumulative hour gains made while circling the globe eastward.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The length of one degree of longitude, measured in kilometres along the ground, is greatest at the
options: Tropic of Cancer
Equator
Poles
Tropic of Capricorn
questions.explanation: Meridians of longitude converge towards the poles, so the ground distance covered by one degree of longitude is largest at the Equator (about 111 km) and shrinks to zero at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbital plane, at approximately 23.5 degrees, directly explains why
options: longitude lines converge at the poles
the Earth's crust is divided into tectonic plates
the Earth completes one rotation every 24 hours
different hemispheres receive varying intensities of sunlight at different times of the year, producing seasons
questions.explanation: Because the axis is tilted, each hemisphere leans towards or away from the sun at different points in the Earth's orbit, changing the angle and duration of sunlight received and producing seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On or around 21 June each year, the Northern Hemisphere experiences its longest day. This event is known as the
options: December solstice
June solstice (summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere)
March equinox
September equinox
questions.explanation: Around 21 June, the North Pole is tilted most directly towards the sun, giving the Northern Hemisphere its longest day of the year, known as the June (summer) solstice.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On or around 22 December each year, the Southern Hemisphere experiences its longest day, while the day and night are most unequal in the Northern Hemisphere. This is known as the
options: December solstice (winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere)
June solstice
September equinox
March equinox
questions.explanation: Around 22 December, the South Pole tilts most directly towards the sun, giving the Southern Hemisphere its longest day, while the Northern Hemisphere experiences its shortest day (winter solstice).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: At the equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September), day and night are of approximately equal length worldwide because
options: the Earth temporarily stops rotating
neither pole is tilted towards or away from the sun, so sunlight is distributed evenly across both hemispheres
the Earth is at its closest point to the sun
the Earth's axis is not tilted at all during these dates
questions.explanation: At the equinoxes, the Earth's axis is tilted sideways relative to the sun rather than towards or away from it, so the terminator line divides day and night equally across all latitudes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Earth's magnetic field, which helps deflect harmful solar radiation, is generated mainly within the
options: liquid outer core
solid inner core
mantle
crust
questions.explanation: Convection currents of molten iron and nickel within the Earth's liquid outer core generate the planet's magnetic field through a process known as the geodynamo effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Compared to oceanic crust, continental crust is generally
options: composed mainly of basalt
thicker and less dense
identical in thickness and density
thinner and denser
questions.explanation: Continental crust is typically thicker (around 30-50 km) and composed of lighter granitic rock, while oceanic crust is thinner and denser, composed mainly of basalt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The approximate circumference of the Earth around the Equator is closest to
questions.explanation: The Earth's equatorial circumference is approximately 40,075 km, a figure historically close to the original definition of the metre (1/10,000,000 of the distance from Equator to pole).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A place located at latitude 40 degrees North and a place at latitude 40 degrees South both lie on lines of latitude that are
options: used to measure time differences directly
identical distances from the North Pole
meridians converging at the poles
parallel to the Equator and to each other
questions.explanation: Lines of latitude (parallels) run parallel to the Equator and to one another; longitude, not latitude, is what determines local time differences.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Basalt, a common igneous rock associated with volcanic eruptions, is classified as
options: extrusive (volcanic), because it cools rapidly at or near the Earth's surface
metamorphic, because it forms under intense pressure
intrusive (plutonic), because it cools slowly deep underground
sedimentary, because it forms from compacted ash layers
questions.explanation: Basalt forms from lava that cools quickly at or near the surface, giving it a fine-grained texture typical of extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks, unlike slow-cooling intrusive rocks such as granite.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes intrusive igneous rocks, such as granite, from extrusive igneous rocks, such as basalt?
options: Intrusive rocks have larger, coarser crystals due to slow cooling underground
Extrusive rocks are always found only underground
Intrusive rocks are formed from compacted sediment
Intrusive rocks always contain visible fossils
questions.explanation: Slow cooling deep within the crust allows large mineral crystals to grow in intrusive rocks like granite, while rapid surface cooling in extrusive rocks like basalt produces much finer crystals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The process by which sedimentary rock layers are compressed and cemented together into solid rock is known as
options: metamorphism
weathering
erosion
lithification
questions.explanation: Lithification is the overall process by which loose sediment is transformed into solid sedimentary rock through compaction and cementation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'strata' in the context of sedimentary rocks?
options: Distinct, parallel layers of sediment deposited over successive periods of time
The molten core of a volcano
Cracks caused by tectonic movement
Individual mineral crystals within an igneous rock
questions.explanation: Strata are the visible, roughly parallel layers within sedimentary rock, each representing a distinct episode or period of sediment deposition.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Slate, a metamorphic rock valued for roofing material, is formed from the metamorphism of
options: shale (a sedimentary rock)
granite (an igneous rock)
limestone (a sedimentary rock)
basalt (an igneous rock)
questions.explanation: Slate forms when shale, a fine-grained sedimentary rock, is subjected to low-grade regional metamorphism, developing its characteristic fine, splittable layering.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Quartzite, a hard metamorphic rock, is formed by the metamorphism of
options: limestone (a sedimentary rock)
sandstone (a sedimentary rock)
shale (a sedimentary rock)
granite (an igneous rock)
questions.explanation: Quartzite forms when sandstone, composed largely of quartz grains, is subjected to heat and pressure, fusing the grains into an extremely hard, interlocking crystalline rock.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: At a convergent (destructive) plate boundary where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the oceanic plate typically
options: subducts (sinks) beneath the less dense continental plate, often forming a deep ocean trench and volcanic activity
moves apart from the continental plate, forming a new mid-ocean ridge
remains completely stationary relative to the continental plate
slides horizontally past the continental plate with no vertical movement
questions.explanation: Because oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, it is forced downward (subducted) beneath the continental plate at convergent boundaries, generating trenches, earthquakes, and volcanic arcs.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: At a divergent (constructive) plate boundary, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, tectonic plates are
options: permanently locked with no relative movement
colliding directly, forming fold mountains
moving apart, with new crust forming as magma rises to fill the gap
sliding horizontally past one another with minimal vertical displacement
questions.explanation: At divergent boundaries, plates move away from each other, and magma rises from the mantle to fill the resulting gap, creating new oceanic crust, as seen along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The San Andreas Fault in California is a classic example of a
options: hotspot unrelated to plate boundaries
convergent boundary with active subduction
transform (conservative) plate boundary, where plates slide horizontally past each other
divergent boundary forming new ocean floor
questions.explanation: The San Andreas Fault marks a transform boundary where the Pacific and North American plates slide past one another horizontally, generating frequent earthquakes without significant crust creation or destruction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Fold mountains, such as the Alps and the Himalayas, are formed primarily as a result of
options: the collision and compression of tectonic plates, causing rock layers to buckle and fold upward
the steady deposition of river sediment over millions of years
wind erosion of a flat plain
volcanic eruptions unrelated to plate movement
questions.explanation: Fold mountains form when compressional forces from colliding tectonic plates squeeze and buckle sedimentary rock layers upward into folds, as with the Himalayas at the India-Eurasia collision zone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An ox-bow lake is a landform formed when
options: a river's mouth deposits sediment to form a triangular plain
a waterfall retreats upstream over geological time
wind erodes a depression in a desert surface
a meander loop is cut off from the main river channel, typically due to erosion narrowing its neck
questions.explanation: As a meander's neck narrows through continued erosion, the river may eventually cut straight across during high flow, isolating the meander loop as a curved ox-bow lake.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A river's 'load' refers to the
options: width of the river channel at its widest point
vertical drop of a river from its source to its mouth
total volume of water flowing past a given point per second
material (sediment, gravel, and dissolved matter) that a river transports along its course
questions.explanation: A river's load is the total quantity of solid and dissolved material it carries, transported through traction, saltation, suspension, and solution.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An escarpment (cuesta) is best described as a
options: circular depression formed by a volcanic crater collapse
flat-topped hill with vertical sides on all sides
narrow, deep valley carved by a fast-flowing river
long, steep slope separating two levels of relatively flat land, often formed by differential erosion of tilted rock strata
questions.explanation: An escarpment forms where gently tilted resistant rock strata are eroded unevenly, leaving a long steep face (scarp slope) and a gentler back slope (dip slope).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following landforms results primarily from chemical weathering of limestone, producing features such as caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage?
options: Barchan dune
Karst landscape
Glacial moraine
Alluvial fan
questions.explanation: Karst landscapes develop where slightly acidic rainwater dissolves soluble limestone over time, creating characteristic surface and underground features such as sinkholes, caverns, and disappearing streams.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A 'barchan' is a specific type of sand dune characterised by
options: a crescent shape with horns pointing in the direction the wind is blowing
a star-shaped mound formed by winds from multiple directions
a long, straight ridge running parallel to the prevailing wind
a shape found exclusively along river banks
questions.explanation: Barchan dunes form in areas with a limited sand supply and a consistent wind direction, producing a distinctive crescent shape with horns extending downwind.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The instrument used to measure the duration of bright sunshine received at a location is the
options: Campbell-Stokes sunshine recorder
barometer
anemometer
hygrometer
questions.explanation: The Campbell-Stokes recorder uses a glass sphere to focus sunlight onto a graduated card, burning a trace that records the duration of bright sunshine each day.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A wind vane is primarily used to indicate
options: wind speed
relative humidity
wind direction
atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: A wind vane freely rotates to align with the wind, pointing in the direction from which the wind is blowing, thereby indicating wind direction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: According to the Koppen climate classification, the Aw (tropical savanna) climate, typical of much of West Africa's Guinea and Sudan zones, is characterised by
options: very low temperatures with permanent snow cover
a short, cool summer with a long, severe winter
high temperatures year-round with a marked alternation between a wet and a dry season
consistently heavy rainfall with no dry season at all
questions.explanation: The Aw climate type experiences high temperatures throughout the year but, unlike the Af (rainforest) type, has a clearly defined dry season alongside a wet season.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Bwh (hot desert) climate type is best characterised by
options: heavy, evenly distributed rainfall year-round
very high daytime temperatures, very low and unreliable rainfall, and a wide diurnal temperature range
permanent cloud cover with minimal sunshine
mild temperatures with a short, dry summer only
questions.explanation: Hot desert climates feature intense daytime heat, very sparse and irregular rainfall, and a large difference between daytime and night-time temperatures due to clear skies and low humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Inter-Tropical Discontinuity (ITD), a key feature in West African climatology, is best described as the
options: line marking the boundary between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres
boundary zone where the moist tropical maritime air mass meets the dry tropical continental air mass
boundary between warm and cold ocean currents
permanent line of high pressure over the Sahara Desert
questions.explanation: The ITD is the surface convergence zone between the moist South-West maritime air mass (bringing rain) and the dry North-East continental (harmattan) air mass, and its seasonal shift drives West Africa's rainfall pattern.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In West Africa, the harmattan wind is best described as a
options: dry, dusty, north-easterly wind blowing from the Sahara Desert, typically occurring between November and March
moist south-westerly wind bringing heavy rainfall throughout the year
warm ocean current flowing along the West African coast
cold polar wind originating from the Southern Ocean
questions.explanation: The harmattan is a dry, dust-laden wind that blows from the Sahara towards the Gulf of Guinea during the dry season, typically reducing visibility and humidity across West Africa.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A warm ocean current flowing along a coastline is most likely to be associated with which climatic effect on the adjoining land?
options: Permanent fog with no effect on temperature
Colder coastal temperatures and desert conditions
Higher coastal temperatures and increased chances of onshore rainfall
No influence at all on coastal temperature or rainfall
questions.explanation: Warm currents raise the temperature of overlying air, increasing its capacity to hold moisture and often enhancing rainfall when onshore winds carry this moist air over the coast.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following ocean currents is a cold current known for contributing to arid coastal conditions in south-western Africa?
options: The Gulf Stream
The Benguela Current
The North Atlantic Drift
The Guinea Current
questions.explanation: The Benguela Current, a cold current flowing northward along the south-western African coast, cools the overlying air and suppresses rainfall, contributing to the aridity of the Namib Desert region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Gulf Stream, a warm ocean current, has which notable effect on the climate of Western Europe?
options: It causes Western Europe to have desert conditions
It has no measurable effect on Western Europe's climate
It contributes to Western Europe's milder winters than would otherwise be expected at its latitude
It causes permanent ice cover along Western Europe's coasts
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream (and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift) carries warm water from the tropics towards North-West Europe, moderating winter temperatures well above what the latitude alone would suggest.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following gases is considered the primary greenhouse gas contributing to anthropogenic (human-caused) global warming?
options: Carbon dioxide
Argon
Nitrogen
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide, released mainly from burning fossil fuels and deforestation, is the primary greenhouse gas driving human-induced global warming, owing to both its heat-trapping properties and large emitted volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Desertification, an increasing environmental concern in the Sudan and Sahel zones of Nigeria, refers to the
options: process of converting a desert into productive farmland through irrigation
process by which fertile or semi-arid land becomes increasingly arid and unproductive, often due to drought and poor land use
increase in rainfall intensity in an already humid tropical zone
gradual cooling of a region's climate leading to glaciation
questions.explanation: Desertification describes land degradation in drylands, typically resulting from a combination of climatic variability (such as prolonged drought) and unsustainable human activities like overgrazing and deforestation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An anticyclone, associated with generally settled, dry weather, is characterised by
options: low atmospheric pressure at its centre with air rising and converging inward
constant, uniform rainfall regardless of season
high atmospheric pressure at its centre with air sinking and diverging outward
the total absence of wind at all times
questions.explanation: An anticyclone is a region of high pressure where air descends and spreads outward near the surface, typically suppressing cloud formation and producing settled, often dry weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The term 'relative humidity' refers to the
options: amount of water vapour in the air expressed as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold at that temperature
difference between the maximum and minimum daily temperature
total volume of water vapour in the air, regardless of temperature
amount of rainfall recorded over a 24-hour period
questions.explanation: Relative humidity expresses the actual moisture content of the air as a percentage of the maximum amount (saturation point) the air could hold at the prevailing temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Convectional rainfall, common in equatorial regions during the afternoon, occurs mainly because
options: warm and cold air masses meet along a frontal boundary
moist air is forced to rise as it crosses a coastline
intense surface heating causes moist air to rise, cool, condense, and fall as heavy, often thundery rain
cold air masses are forced to rise over a mountain range
questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall results from strong surface heating (typical of equatorial afternoons), which causes moist air to rise rapidly, cool adiabatically, condense into cumulonimbus clouds, and produce intense showers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Orographic (relief) rainfall occurs when
options: air descends and warms on the leeward side of a mountain
warm, moist air rises purely due to intense surface heating
two air masses of different temperatures converge along a front
moist air is forced to rise over a mountain or highland barrier, cooling and condensing on the windward side
questions.explanation: Orographic rainfall occurs when moist air is forced upward by a topographic barrier such as a mountain range, cooling as it rises and releasing precipitation mainly on the windward slope.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An ecosystem is best defined as a
options: collection of plant species found within a single country
region defined solely by its political boundaries
list of all animal species found on Earth
community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (physical) environment
questions.explanation: An ecosystem encompasses both the biotic (living) community and the abiotic (non-living) physical environment, along with the interactions and energy flows between them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In an ecological food chain, 'producers' are organisms that
options: synthesise their own food, typically through photosynthesis, forming the base of the chain
consume only other animals
break down dead organic matter into simpler substances
occupy the highest trophic level in the chain
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis, forming the essential first trophic level upon which all consumers depend.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: 'Decomposers' in an ecosystem play the essential role of
options: converting atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can absorb, exclusively
capturing solar energy directly through photosynthesis
occupying the top of the food chain as apex predators
breaking down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the soil for reuse by producers
questions.explanation: Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead plant and animal matter, recycling essential nutrients back into the soil where they become available again to producers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Deforestation in tropical regions such as Nigeria's rainforest belt commonly leads to which of the following environmental consequences?
options: A permanent decrease in local temperatures
Increased soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, and disruption of local rainfall patterns
An increase in groundwater recharge with no other effects
Increased soil fertility with no negative environmental impact
questions.explanation: Removing forest cover exposes soil to erosion, destroys wildlife habitats (reducing biodiversity), and can disrupt local evapotranspiration cycles that contribute to rainfall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Soil erosion by water is generally most severe on
options: steep slopes with little or no vegetation cover
well-vegetated river deltas
areas with permanent snow cover
flat plains with dense grass cover
questions.explanation: Steep, bare slopes offer little resistance to the erosive force of surface runoff, allowing water to strip away topsoil far more readily than on flat, well-vegetated land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Gully erosion, a severe form of soil erosion notably widespread in parts of south-eastern Nigeria, is best described as
options: the formation of large, deep channels cut into the land surface by concentrated surface runoff
the wearing away of a coastline by wave action
the deposition of sediment at a river's mouth
the gradual, uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil across a wide area
questions.explanation: Gully erosion occurs when concentrated flows of water cut progressively deeper and wider channels into the land, a process notably severe in areas like Anambra and Imo States in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary human-induced cause of desert encroachment (desertification) in Nigeria's far north?
options: Overgrazing and excessive cutting of vegetation for fuelwood, combined with recurrent drought
A sudden drop in regional temperature causing permafrost to form
Volcanic ash deposits smothering vegetation
Excessive and prolonged rainfall over many decades
questions.explanation: In Nigeria's far north, overgrazing, fuelwood harvesting, and unsustainable farming practices, compounded by recurrent drought, strip vegetation cover and accelerate the southward advance of desert-like conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Biodiversity conservation strategies such as establishing national parks and game reserves primarily aim to
options: eliminate all human access to a given area permanently
maximise short-term agricultural output from the land
protect natural habitats and preserve species and genetic diversity
increase the rate of deforestation for controlled study
questions.explanation: Protected areas such as national parks safeguard natural habitats from destructive human activity, helping to preserve species populations and overall genetic and ecological diversity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of mangrove forests found along Nigeria's coastline?
options: They primarily function to increase soil salinity in farmland
They stabilise the coastline against erosion and provide breeding grounds for fish and other marine life
They are found only in freshwater environments far from the coast
They have no ecological function and can be cleared without any environmental consequence
questions.explanation: Mangrove forests bind coastal sediments with their dense root systems, reducing erosion, while also serving as vital nursery habitats for fish, shellfish, and other marine species.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Oil spillage in the Niger Delta region has had which of the following significant environmental impacts?
options: Contamination of soil and water, destruction of aquatic life, and loss of farmland productivity
No measurable impact on local vegetation or water quality
A general improvement in soil fertility across the region
An increase in the population of freshwater fish species
questions.explanation: Crude oil spills in the Niger Delta have repeatedly contaminated soils and waterways, killing aquatic organisms, degrading mangrove ecosystems, and undermining local farming and fishing livelihoods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The greenhouse gas 'methane', a significant contributor to global warming, is released substantially from
options: the depletion of the ozone layer directly
volcanic ash clouds exclusively
livestock digestion, rice paddies, and decomposing organic waste in landfills
the combustion of coal exclusively
questions.explanation: Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, is released from anaerobic digestion in livestock, flooded rice paddies, and decomposing organic waste in landfills, in addition to fossil fuel extraction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best explains the ecological concept of a 'food web'?
options: A diagram showing only the predator-prey relationship between two species
An interconnected network of multiple overlapping food chains within an ecosystem
A list of all decomposers found in a particular habitat
A single, linear sequence showing energy flow from producer to top consumer
questions.explanation: A food web represents the complex, interlinked feeding relationships among many species in an ecosystem, capturing the reality that most organisms have multiple food sources and predators, unlike a single food chain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The depletion of the ozone layer in the stratosphere has historically been linked most strongly to the release of
options: water vapour from ocean evaporation
carbon dioxide from fossil fuel combustion
methane from livestock
chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
questions.explanation: Chlorofluorocarbons, once widely used in refrigerants and aerosol propellants, release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone molecules, thinning the protective ozone layer.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Sustainable development, as applied to environmental management, is best defined as development that
options: meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
maximises immediate economic profit regardless of long-term environmental cost
prohibits all forms of resource extraction permanently
focuses exclusively on industrial growth with no regard for natural resources
questions.explanation: This widely used definition of sustainable development balances present-day economic and social needs against the responsibility to preserve resources and environmental quality for future generations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: According to demographic transition theory, a country in the 'early expanding' stage typically has
options: equal, very high birth and death rates, producing minimal net growth
both low birth rates and low death rates, producing minimal population growth
a low birth rate and a high death rate, producing population decline
a high birth rate and a rapidly falling death rate, producing rapid population growth
questions.explanation: In the early expanding stage, improvements in healthcare and sanitation cause death rates to fall sharply while birth rates remain high, resulting in a period of rapid population growth.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Population density is calculated as the
options: total number of settlements within a region
birth rate minus the death rate of a region
total land area divided by the total population
total population of an area divided by the total land area
questions.explanation: Population density expresses how crowded an area is, calculated by dividing the total number of people by the total land area, usually expressed as persons per square kilometre.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A country's 'natural increase' in population is calculated as the
options: birth rate plus the death rate
immigration rate minus the emigration rate
birth rate minus the death rate
total population divided by land area
questions.explanation: Natural increase measures population change due purely to births and deaths, calculated as the birth rate minus the death rate, excluding the effects of migration.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rural-urban migration in Nigeria has been driven mainly by
options: the complete absence of any agricultural activity in rural areas
government policies actively restricting movement into rural areas
a general decline in urban population growth rates
the perceived availability of better employment, education, and social amenities in urban areas
questions.explanation: Rural-urban migration in Nigeria, as in much of the developing world, is largely driven by 'pull' factors such as perceived better job opportunities, education, healthcare, and infrastructure in cities.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is a common consequence of rapid, unplanned urbanisation in Nigerian cities?
options: The growth of slums and informal settlements with inadequate infrastructure
A uniform and immediate improvement in housing quality for all residents
A decrease in traffic congestion
The elimination of unemployment within the urban area
questions.explanation: When urban population growth outpaces planned housing and infrastructure development, informal settlements and slums often emerge, characterised by overcrowding and inadequate services.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Shifting cultivation, a traditional farming system practised in parts of tropical Africa, involves
options: permanently cultivating a single, heavily fertilised plot of land year after year
clearing and cultivating a plot of land for a few years before abandoning it to fallow and moving to a new plot
large-scale, mechanised cultivation of a single cash crop for export only
cultivation exclusively on irrigated desert land
questions.explanation: Shifting cultivation involves farming a cleared plot until soil fertility declines, then abandoning it to natural regrowth (fallow) while a new plot is cleared, allowing the original soil to regenerate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'commercial (plantation) agriculture' as practised in parts of Nigeria, such as oil palm and rubber estates?
options: Farming practised only on unimproved, unfenced communal land
Large-scale cultivation of a single cash crop primarily for sale and export, often using hired labour
Small-scale farming intended solely for household (subsistence) consumption
Cultivation of multiple food crops solely for local subsistence needs
questions.explanation: Plantation agriculture is characterised by large-scale monoculture of a cash crop, substantial capital investment, and hired labour, with output destined mainly for sale rather than direct household consumption.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Transhumance, a form of pastoral farming practised by groups such as the Fulani in Nigeria, involves
options: cultivating crops exclusively without any livestock rearing
permanently keeping livestock enclosed within a single fixed ranch
fishing as the primary and sole economic activity
the seasonal movement of livestock between fixed grazing areas in search of pasture and water
questions.explanation: Transhumance involves herders moving livestock seasonally, often southward in the dry season and northward in the wet season, between established grazing grounds to access adequate pasture and water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following industries is classified as a 'primary' economic activity?
options: Crude oil extraction
Vehicle assembly
Banking services
Retail trading
questions.explanation: Primary economic activities involve the direct extraction or harvesting of natural resources, such as crude oil extraction, mining, farming, and fishing, distinguishing them from manufacturing (secondary) or service (tertiary) activities.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a 'secondary' economic activity from a 'tertiary' one?
options: Secondary activities involve manufacturing or processing raw materials into finished goods, while tertiary activities provide services
There is no meaningful distinction between the two categories
Secondary activities involve only the extraction of raw materials from nature
Tertiary activities involve only agricultural production
questions.explanation: Secondary activities transform raw materials into manufactured products (e.g., processing crude oil into refined fuel), while tertiary activities involve providing services, such as transport, banking, and retail.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A 'primate city', a concept relevant to Nigeria's urban hierarchy historically centred on Lagos, refers to a city that is
options: disproportionately larger and more economically dominant than any other city in the country
defined strictly by having the lowest population density nationwide
located exclusively in a country's rural interior
the smallest settlement within a country's urban hierarchy
questions.explanation: A primate city dominates a country's urban system in population and economic influence, being disproportionately larger than the second-largest city, a role historically held by Lagos in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the economic significance of the trans-Saharan trade routes historically linking West Africa to North Africa?
options: They facilitated the exchange of goods such as gold, salt, and slaves between West and North Africa
They were established only in the twentieth century for oil transport
They connected West Africa directly to the Americas by an overland route
They were used exclusively for the movement of livestock and had no commercial function
questions.explanation: For centuries before European maritime trade, caravan routes across the Sahara enabled the exchange of West African gold and slaves for North African salt, cloth, and other goods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following transport modes is generally most cost-effective for moving bulky goods, such as crude oil, over long distances?
options: Pipeline transport
Air transport
Human porterage
Road transport by truck
questions.explanation: Pipelines offer continuous, low-cost transport of large volumes of liquids or gases such as crude oil and natural gas over long distances, generally cheaper per unit than road or air transport for such bulky cargo.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A 'push factor' in migration studies refers to a condition that
options: drives people to leave their place of origin, such as unemployment, conflict, or poor social amenities
applies only to international, not internal, migration
attracts people to a destination area, such as better job prospects
prevents any migration from occurring at all
questions.explanation: Push factors are unfavourable conditions in a migrant's place of origin, such as unemployment, insecurity, or lack of services, that motivate them to leave, as distinct from 'pull' factors attracting them elsewhere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Nigeria is located on the continent of Africa, lying roughly between which of the following latitude ranges?
options: About 4 degrees South and 14 degrees South
About 60 degrees North and 70 degrees North
About 30 degrees North and 40 degrees North
About 4 degrees North and 14 degrees North
questions.explanation: Nigeria lies entirely within the Northern Hemisphere's tropics, extending roughly from about 4 degrees North near the coast to about 14 degrees North near its northern border.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which West African country shares Nigeria's eastern border?
options: Niger Republic
Chad
Benin Republic
Cameroon
questions.explanation: Cameroon lies directly to the east of Nigeria, while Benin Republic lies to the west, Niger Republic to the north, and Nigeria also shares a short north-eastern boundary with Chad near Lake Chad.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the general relief of the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria?
options: A low-lying coastal plain below 50 metres elevation
An active volcanic region with recent lava flows
An extensive highland area with an average elevation above 1,200 metres, formed largely of ancient crystalline rocks
A permanently flooded river floodplain
questions.explanation: The Jos Plateau is a prominent highland region in central Nigeria, rising well above the surrounding lowlands, formed mainly of ancient Precambrian basement complex rocks, and historically significant for tin mining.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: River Niger and River Benue, Nigeria's two major rivers, converge (meet) at which Nigerian city?
options: Jebba
Onitsha
Yola
Lokoja
questions.explanation: The River Niger and River Benue meet at the confluence town of Lokoja in Kogi State, a geographically and historically significant location in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Niger Delta, Nigeria's major oil-producing region, is best classified geographically as an example of a
options: semi-arid zone with sparse vegetation
mountainous region with steep, forested slopes
high plateau region with cool temperatures
large, low-lying river delta with extensive mangrove swamps
questions.explanation: The Niger Delta is one of the world's largest river deltas, characterised by low-lying, swampy terrain, extensive mangrove forests, and a dense network of distributary channels and creeks.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Nigeria's climate, moving from the coast in the south to the far north, generally transitions through which sequence of vegetation belts?
options: Temperate grassland, tundra, and then rainforest
Desert, then rainforest, then temperate forest
Sahel savanna, guinea savanna, sudan savanna, and mangrove forest
Mangrove/rainforest, guinea savanna, sudan savanna, and sahel savanna
questions.explanation: Nigeria's vegetation shifts from coastal mangrove and rainforest in the south, through guinea savanna and sudan savanna in the middle belt and north, to sahel savanna near the far northern border, reflecting decreasing rainfall northward.
